analysis.one_liner: Repeals federal background checks for gun buyers and the federal assault weapons ban.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by Rep. Ron Paul and 3 cosponsors, never got a hearing or a vote and died in a House Judiciary subcommittee when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Ron Paul's bill would wipe two major federal gun laws off the books: the Brady Act, which requires background checks before most gun sales, and the 1994 ban on making and selling assault weapons. It would also delete rules that restrict certain guns to 'sporting purposes,' widening what can legally be sold. Everything would take effect immediately.
analysis.who_benefits: Gun owners gain the ability to buy firearms — including newly made assault weapons — with no federal background check. Firearms manufacturers and dealers shed the Brady Act's record-keeping and screening duties and regain the assault-weapon product line.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act, ending the federal requirement that licensed dealers run background checks on buyers, and restores the law as it was before 1993 [S2][S3].
Repeals Title XI of the 1994 crime law — the Public Safety and Recreational Firearms Use Protection Act, the federal ban on assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition magazines [S2][S3].
Strikes the 'sporting purposes' language from federal firearms and gun-control statutes, so guns no longer have to be deemed suitable for sport to be legal to make, sell, or import [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public bears whatever added risk comes from gun sales with no background check — people legally barred from buying guns, such as convicted felons and domestic abusers, could purchase without being screened — and from assault weapons and large-capacity magazines returning to legal sale.

drawbacks.text: Ending the Brady Act would remove the federal screen that stops prohibited buyers — felons, domestic abusers, and others — from buying guns from licensed dealers [S2][S3].
Repealing the 1994 ban would again allow manufacture and sale of semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, which police groups opposed as a safety risk [S2][S3].
The bill would revive older statutes as if the two laws had never passed, an immediate and sweeping rewrite of federal gun rules with no transition period [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a real, immediate gain to gun owners — no background checks and a wider legal market — but it does so by deleting two federal safety systems at once, with no transition or replacement screening. Honest supporters would have to acknowledge that the same change that frees lawful buyers also removes the check on prohibited ones.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2001, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, then to its Crime Subcommittee a few weeks later, and sat there until the 107th Congress ended in January 2003 with no hearing, no markup, and no vote [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Paul introduced the bill on May 8, 2001, with 3 cosponsors (2 Republicans, 1 Democrat) [S1][S4][S5].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never acted on it [S1][S5].
On May 30, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, where it remained without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Supporters of federal gun regulation are better off because the bill died: the Brady background-check system and the assault weapons ban stayed on the books, and the firearms industry did not gain its expanded market.

for.name: Rep. Ron Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and framed it as restoring Second Amendment rights for all Americans

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner (R-WI) at the time
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Crime Subcommittee and never scheduled a hearing or markup during the two-year Congress

against.name: Subcommittee on Crime
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from May 2001 until the Congress ended with no action

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was nearly all Republican — 2 of 3 cosponsors were Republicans, with a single Democratic cosponsor — and the bill drew no floor action in either chamber [S4][S5].

industries.note: Repealing the Brady Act would free licensed dealers from background-check and record duties, and repeal of the 1994 ban would reopen the market for assault weapons and large-capacity magazines. The industry's gain comes from removing the screening that stands between prohibited buyers and gun sales.
